title: 'If thou must love me'
short: The speaker asks to be loved for no reason at all except love itself, since every reason can change.
body: The conditional 'If thou must' carries the reluctance of the early sonnets, in which the speaker doubts she is worthy of Browning's love. 'For nought / Except for love's sake only' means for no cause outside love. The argument is a familiar one in love poetry (love that depends on qualities ends when the qualities change), but Barrett's turn is to forbid even the most flattering reasons. The sonnet is one of the best known of the sequence, often anthologised and set to music.

anchor: I love her for her smile
title: the rejected reasons
short: The imagined lover's reasons (smile, look, way of speaking, a sympathetic thought) are all ruled out.
body: Barrett ventriloquises a lover listing the beloved's charms, a gentle refusal of the blazon, the catalogue of the beloved's features in Petrarchan poetry. But the charms here are of manner rather than body: smile, look, 'way / Of speaking gently', 'a trick of thought / That falls in well with mine'. 'Trick' here means habit or characteristic turn, not deceit. The passage pointedly sets aside the conventions of love poetry by having the woman refuse them.

sources.cite: Sandra Donaldson (gen. ed.), The Works of Elizabeth Barrett Browning, 5 vols (Pickering & Chatto, 2010), Sonnets from the Portuguese, notes

title: certes
short: 'Certes' is an archaic word meaning 'certainly, assuredly'.
body: Barrett's diction mixes everyday speech with archaisms like 'certes' (from Old French), used by Chaucer and Spenser. The effect is half-playful, giving the imagined lover's praise ('certes brought / A sense of pleasant ease on such a day') a mock-courtly flavour, as if he were remembering a particular afternoon visit. The Brownings' courtship was conducted largely through letters and brief visits to her room in Wimpole Street, where such moments of 'pleasant ease' mattered.

sources.cite: The Brownings' Correspondence (Baylor University / Wedgestone Press), online edition

anchor: Be changed, or change for thee
title: 'Be changed, or change for thee'
short: Qualities may themselves change, or may seem changed to the lover; love built on them can be undone the same way.
body: The alternative 'Be changed, or change for thee' distinguishes two dangers: the beloved's qualities may actually alter, or the lover's perception of them may. Love 'so wrought, / May be unwrought so', made by reasons and unmade by them. 'Wrought' (made, worked) and 'unwrought' are a craftsman's terms. The argument recalls Shakespeare's Sonnet 116, 'Love is not love / Which alters when it alteration finds', which Barrett's lines seem to answer from the beloved's side.

sources.cite: Shakespeare, Sonnet 116, ll. 2-3 ('Love is not love / Which alters when it alteration finds')

title: pity wiping my cheeks dry
short: She also forbids him to love her out of pity, since comfort might end her tears and so end his love.
body: Barrett had been an invalid for years, and much of the sequence fears that Browning's love is compassion for a sick, grieving woman. Here she argues that a woman long comforted might 'forget to weep', and if pity were the cause of love, the love would then cease. The phrase 'A creature' modestly describes herself as any living being. The logic is witty and anxious at once: happiness itself could cost her his love.

title: love's eternity
short: Only love for love's sake can last 'evermore', since nothing outside it can change.
body: The final couplet-like sentence returns to the opening phrase 'love's sake' and adds 'love on, through love's eternity'. The word 'love' appears six times in the last six lines, a deliberate saturation. The religious idea that love is eternal (cf. 1 Corinthians 13:8, 'Charity never faileth') underlies the close. Some critics find the ending abstract; others note how the speaker, after refusing all particular reasons, finally claims for herself the most generous reason of all.

sources.cite: Sandra Donaldson (gen. ed.), The Works of Elizabeth Barrett Browning, 5 vols (Pickering & Chatto, 2010), Sonnets from the Portuguese, notes

title: Form: Petrarchan rhyme, broken lines
short: A Petrarchan sonnet whose volta falls mid-line, the sentence 'Neither love me for' running into the next line.
body: The octave rhymes abbaabba on 'nought/thought/brought/wrought' and 'say/way/day/may'; the sestet rhymes 'for/bore/evermore' with 'dry/thereby/eternity', a cdcdcd pattern. The turn comes mid-line 9 with a full stop and a new sentence ending on the weak word 'for', a strong enjambment. Barrett's sonnets were sometimes criticised for such roughness; recent critics read it as a conscious effect, giving speech-like urgency to a strict form.
